where: Section 3, transition delay fault paragraph and exam trap 5
problem: The roles of launch and capture are swapped. In standard usage the launch edge/vector is the one that creates the transition at the line under test, and the capture edge/clock captures the response after the rated clock period. The chapter says the launch vector sets the initial value and the capture vector creates the transition, which contradicts every standard treatment and will make a student write the wrong definition in the exam.
fix: The test uses a vector pair and two clock edges: the first vector sets the line to its initial value, the launch clock edge creates the transition, and the capture clock edge captures the response after the rated clock period. If the path is too slow, the captured value is the old one.

problem: 'a stem fault can be equivalent to branch faults' is too loose. A stem fault is equivalent to the multiple fault in which all fanout branches are stuck at the same value, not to one branch fault. A student may conclude that one branch fault represents the stem.
fix: With fanout, a stem fault is equivalent to the multiple fault in which every fanout branch is stuck at the same value, so test programs place checkpoints on the fanout branches and do not count the stem again.

problem: 'disconnect the output from supply' names only one rail. In static CMOS a stuck-open transistor can disconnect the output from VDD or from ground, depending on whether the broken transistor is in the pull-up or the pull-down network.
fix: In static CMOS, a stuck-open may disconnect the output from the positive supply (VDD) or from ground for one input combination.

problem: 'A stuck-open in CMOS can pass a single-vector test' is ambiguous: 'pass a test' can be read as 'is detected by the test', which is the opposite of the intended meaning.
fix: A stuck-open in CMOS can escape a single-vector test; it often needs a two-vector sequence because the floating output keeps its old value.

where: Section 3, last sentence on redundant faults
problem: The redundant-fault definition is dropped into the delay-fault paragraph, although redundancy is mainly a stuck-at concept, and the wording suggests these faults are known and deleted before any tool runs. Redundancy is normally proved by ATPG.
fix: Move the point to Section 2 and say: a redundant fault has no vector that detects it; ATPG identifies such faults and they are excluded from the fault list before fault coverage is computed.
